title: The First Mail from Home
body: The dak brings it in one bundle: your mother’s hand, your sister’s, a line from your tutor who coached you for the competition. They are a month old and smell faintly of the sea. Your mother has underlined nothing and asked everything; your sister wants to know if you have shot a tiger yet; the tutor observes that the Service is a marathon and hopes you are eating. On the desk between you and the answer lie forty unfiled petitions and the whole of the evening.

choices.label: Give them the whole evening: four pages, honestly.
choices.outcome: You tell them nearly all of it — the camp at dawn, the tahsildar’s patience, the size of the sky, the smallness of yourself — and something unknots between your shoulders as you write. The letters will take a month to arrive and be read aloud twice at Home, and you will keep this habit, mail by mail, and it will quietly help to save you.

choices.label: A cheerful page each, and back to the petitions.
choices.outcome: Three bright, dutiful pages that read like a boy doing his correspondence, because they are. The petitions get their evening; the Service approves of men who clear their tables. Your mother reads between every line, as mothers do, and begins a letter about eating properly.

choices.label: Put them in the drawer to answer properly ‘when there is time.’
choices.outcome: There is never time; there is only the choosing of it, which nobody has taught you yet. The bundle goes into the drawer with its string uncut, and the next mail’s bundle goes in on top of it, and something eleven thousand miles long begins, very slowly, to fray.

title: The Girl at the Christmas Camp
body: She is out from Home for the cold weather — a judge’s niece, sensible and quick, with a seat on a horse that shames half the station and a way of asking what a cutcherry actually does that suggests she wants the real answer. For six days of the Week you are thrown together by every hostess in the district, the juniormost officer and the visiting niece, and on the seventh day there is a paper-chase, and you ride it side by side, and it is suddenly not a small thing at all. She sails for Home in March. Everyone is watching, because at a station everyone always is.

choices.label: Ask leave to write to her.
choices.outcome: ‘You may write,’ she says, before you have finished asking — and you learn something of how the week looked from her side of it. The station smiles behind its hands for a fortnight; the Collector’s wife begins to plan. A probationer with an understanding at Home is reckoned half-steadied already, and the mail, from March, will matter more than it has ever mattered.

choices.label: Say nothing; a probationer has no business with an understanding.
choices.outcome: It is the correct, careful, Service answer, and you give it to yourself in the shaving-glass on the morning she leaves for the railway. She looks back once from the tonga. You will be confirmed, in due course, in the Service and in the habit that answer began — and of the two confirmations, the second will cost you more.

choices.label: Say too much, too soon, on the last evening.
choices.outcome: Moonlight, the band, six days of it behind you, and you make the speech a man should make after six months, not six days. She is kinder about it than you deserve, and the story is round the station by the following tiffin, told gently, at your expense. ‘They are all the same, out from Home,’ says the Collector’s wife — and for once the verandah does not argue with her.

consult.opinion: The Collector, mellow over the second peg, is nearly human. ‘Write to her, boy. A probationer with someone at Home writes fewer fool letters and drinks fewer pegs — I know, I was one.’ He does not add the rest: that March to March is a long post, and that half the understandings struck in Christmas Week do not last out the first hot weather. He has watched a good many girls sail.

title: A Parcel from Home
body: It has been three months on the water and a fortnight in the dak: a cake in a tin, packed by your mother against every ordinance of climate and distance. One end is mould and must be cut away with ceremony; the rest is Christmas at nine thousand miles’ remove, eaten slowly on the verandah with the jackals tuning up beyond the compound wall. The tahsildar, offered a slice, pronounces it excellent, and quite unlike food. You keep the tin. Everyone keeps the tin.

title: The First Loo
body: You had been told about the loo the way you had been told about everything — at Home, at dinner, by men leaning back from the table — and none of it is the thing itself: a wind out of a kiln at ten in the morning, the sky gone white, the birds silent, a heat that leans on the shutters like a creditor. You work in the brown dark behind wetted screens and understand, for the first time and permanently, that this country is not exaggerated. The old men at Home were not telling stories. They were leaving things out.
